This section examines Scaling and
applications (5–6 minutes) from first

principles. Keep two questions separate:
does changing the order change

the measured outcome, and does the
proposed search method beat

a matched alternative at the same
distinct-evaluation budget? Explain the

proposed three-stage weight-sharing
strategy: pre-train a compatible

supernet once; freeze shared weights and
score many orderings cheaply;

retrain or fine-tune only the top k
orderings from scratch.

Clearly label this as a scaling proposal,
not a completed

result in the supplied paper. Show target
domains as concrete

ordering variables rather than speculative
icons: LLM/SLM

reasoning-instruction order; SciML
preprocessing and discovery steps;

compiler optimization passes; molecular
operation sequences; neural block

placement. For every domain, display
“fixed components,” “variable order,”

and “fitness measurement.” Do not attach
quantitative expected improvements

unless they were actually measured. The
distinction is part of

the result. A large ordering effect does
not automatically imply

an evolutionary-search advantage, and
